messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Keanu traces the spreadsheet on his screen with a finger, but the numbers blur into a meaningless grid. It has been eighteen months since the night the ocean came into their house. He remembers the silence first. Not a complete silence, but the eerie cessation of the normal night sounds—the crickets, the distant road noise—replaced by a low, guttural hum that seemed to come from the earth itself. He and his wife, Leilani, had been on the lanai, sharing a moment of quiet contentment after dinner. That feeling of peace is now one of his most potent triggers; any flicker of happiness or relaxation sends a jolt of pure panic through him, a certainty that catastrophe is imminent. He has learned to avoid relaxing, filling every moment with work or distracting noise. He keeps the television on all night, because waking up in the dark is unbearable, instantly plunging him back into the black, churning water.

The memory of that night is not a story he can tell. When his well-meaning sister-in-law tried to talk to him about it, the words caught in his throat. How could he explain something that still feels so profoundly unreal, like a film he’d been forced to watch? The memory arrives not in narrative but in fragments of raw sensation. Sometimes, while reviewing a client’s inventory in a sterile, air-conditioned office, he is suddenly overwhelmed by the thick, cloying smell of saltwater and decay. More than once, the taste of briny grit has filled his mouth so vividly that he has had to run to the restroom, spitting into the sink. These sensory intrusions are stark reminders of a reality so extreme it feels impossible that he survived it, and that Leilani did not. The world, he has come to understand, is simply a dangerous place, and he is powerless to stop the terrible things from happening.

This belief now governs his life. As an auditor, his job requires meticulous attention to detail and risk assessment, a skill set that has now metastasized into his personal life. He avoids any unfamiliar places, turning down new client engagements if they require him to visit a location he hasn't personally vetted for structural soundness and clear escape routes. His manager is beginning to notice. Last week, a project meeting was delayed by twenty minutes, and Keanu found himself sweating, his heart hammering in his chest, convinced the delay was a precursor to some awful event. Even unusual silence at the office, like when the HVAC system briefly cycles off, makes him feel a primal sense of dread, as if the world is holding its breath before another devastating roar. He feels hollowed out, as though the part of him that could feel joy or connection was washed away that night. He often tells himself he feels dead inside, a walking ghost in his own life.

His routines have become rigid, designed to minimize risk and sensation. He takes the same route to work, eats the same lunch, and speaks to colleagues only when necessary. He has picked up smoking again, the sharp burn in his lungs a controllable, predictable sensation that anchors him to the present. The habit gives him a reason to step outside, to stand alone, to not have to engage. It was after a particularly bad week, when a moment of unexpected laughter with a colleague triggered a full-blown panic attack, that Keanu realized he could not continue this way. The terror of feeling good was more exhausting than the grief itself. He didn’t come to therapy to find happiness—that concept feels both naive and terrifying. He came because he is tired of being afraid of silence, of the dark, of a delayed train, and most of all, of the memory of his own fleeting joy.
